name: requests
requirements: I'm a backend developer who calls requests every day. Show me how requests.get() becomes an HTTP request, and where sessions and adapters fit in.

stops.caption: The library code lives in src/requests, with tests in tests and docs in docs. We start at help.py, rank 1, which imports the package __init__ and is tested by test_help.py.
stops.title: src/requests/help.py

stops.caption: _types.py holds shared type definitions, such as the keyword-argument types for requests. Adapters, models, sessions and utils all import it. Next: adapters.py.
stops.title: src/requests/_types.py

stops.caption: adapters.py defines BaseAdapter and HTTPAdapter. An adapter is the layer a session hands requests to. Let's look at HTTPAdapter.
stops.title: src/requests/adapters.py

stops.caption: HTTPAdapter extends BaseAdapter and links to Response, CaseInsensitiveDict and RequestException. Session uses it, which we'll see soon.
stops.title: HTTPAdapter

stops.caption: structures.py provides CaseInsensitiveDict and LookupDict, helper data structures. Nine files import it, including models, sessions and adapters.
stops.title: src/requests/structures.py

stops.caption: sessions.py defines SessionRedirectMixin (a mixin is a class that adds reusable behavior) and Session. Next: the Session class.
stops.title: src/requests/sessions.py

stops.caption: Session inherits from SessionRedirectMixin and connects Request, PreparedRequest and HTTPAdapter. This is where those pieces come together.
stops.title: Session

stops.caption: models.py defines Request, PreparedRequest and Response, and 11 files import it. Remember the Session → HTTPAdapter → Response path. Read hooks.py and utils.py next.
stops.title: src/requests/models.py

ranking.query: Understand the application architecture, main entry points, core modules, configuration, dependencies, and how to load, process and return data.

questions.question: A maintainer asks a user to run this module before filing an issue. What job does it do for them?
questions.answer: It gathers the platform, Python implementation and installed dependency versions into one report and prints it as JSON
distractors: It checks installed dependency versions and raises an error if any of them is unsupported
It sends a test HTTP request and reports whether the user's network and TLS setup work
It installs any missing optional dependencies so the user can reproduce the bug
choices: It checks installed dependency versions and raises an error if any of them is unsupported
It sends a test HTTP request and reports whether the user's network and TLS setup work
It installs any missing optional dependencies so the user can reproduce the bug
It gathers the platform, Python implementation and installed dependency versions into one report and prints it as JSON
questions.explanation: The module docstring calls it a bug report helper; info() builds a dict of platform, implementation and library versions and main() prints it with json.dumps (src/requests/help.py:1, src/requests/help.py:67, src/requests/help.py:128). It never rejects versions, makes requests or installs anything; version enforcement lives elsewhere in the package.

questions.concept: How the encoding-detector flag is derived
questions.question: A bug report shows "using_charset_normalizer": false, yet the user insists charset_normalizer is installed. What is the most likely explanation?
questions.answer: chardet is also installed; the flag is computed from whether chardet is missing, matching the package's preference for chardet when both exist
distractors: The charset_normalizer import failed, so the helper set it to None and reported false
The flag reflects whether charset_normalizer passed the version check in check_compatibility
info() reports false whenever pyOpenSSL is in use, because the two features are exclusive
choices: chardet is also installed; the flag is computed from whether chardet is missing, matching the package's preference for chardet when both exist
info() reports false whenever pyOpenSSL is in use, because the two features are exclusive
The charset_normalizer import failed, so the helper set it to None and reported false
The flag reflects whether charset_normalizer passed the version check in check_compatibility
questions.explanation: The flag is set as `chardet is None`, not from charset_normalizer itself (src/requests/help.py:113), and the package's compatibility check also looks at chardet first and only falls back to charset_normalizer (src/requests/__init__.py:81-90). If the import had failed, the separate charset_normalizer version entry would be None, so the user should look at that field rather than assume the import broke.

questions.concept: Type guard that is a no-op at runtime
questions.question: A PreparedRequest whose url is still None is passed to is_prepared() in a normal (non-type-checking) run. What happens?
questions.answer: It returns True; the url/method check only exists for static type checkers
distractors: It returns False because url is None
It raises an AssertionError explaining the request was not prepared
It calls prepare() on the request to fill in the missing url
choices: It raises an AssertionError explaining the request was not prepared
It returns True; the url/method check only exists for static type checkers
It returns False because url is None
It calls prepare() on the request to fill in the missing url
questions.explanation: At runtime TYPE_CHECKING is False, so the function skips the url/method check and returns True; the comment says it is a no-op to avoid an AssertionError (src/requests/_types.py:47-52). The check on line 50 is only seen by type checkers, so it never returns False or raises at runtime.

questions.question: HTTPAdapter.build_response starts with `assert _is_prepared(req)` and then reads req.url. What does this assert do in practice?
questions.answer: It tells the type checker req is a _ValidatedRequest so req.url and req.method are str, while never failing at runtime
distractors: It stops a request with no url at runtime before a Response is built
It converts req into a _ValidatedRequest instance so later code can rely on url being set
It is how build_response detects a redirect that needs to be re-prepared
choices: It converts req into a _ValidatedRequest instance so later code can rely on url being set
It tells the type checker req is a _ValidatedRequest so req.url and req.method are str, while never failing at runtime
It is how build_response detects a redirect that needs to be re-prepared
It stops a request with no url at runtime before a Response is built
questions.explanation: is_prepared returns TypeIs[_ValidatedRequest], and _ValidatedRequest redeclares url and method as str (src/requests/_types.py:47, 69-79). At runtime it always returns True (line 52), so the assert in src/requests/adapters.py:375 never fires and nothing is converted.

questions.question: BaseAdapter's send() and close() only raise NotImplementedError. What role does BaseAdapter play in this module?
questions.answer: It defines the contract every transport adapter must fulfil — take a PreparedRequest and return a Response, and clean up — while concrete classes like HTTPAdapter supply the actual connection logic.
distractors: It is a fallback adapter that Requests uses when HTTPAdapter fails, so raising NotImplementedError signals that the request should be retried.
It manages the urllib3 connection pool shared by all adapters, and send() is left unimplemented because pooling happens in __init__.
It is a deprecated class kept only for backward compatibility, and its methods raise to stop anyone from calling them.
choices: It defines the contract every transport adapter must fulfil — take a PreparedRequest and return a Response, and clean up — while concrete classes like HTTPAdapter supply the actual connection logic.
It is a fallback adapter that Requests uses when HTTPAdapter fails, so raising NotImplementedError signals that the request should be retried.
It is a deprecated class kept only for backward compatibility, and its methods raise to stop anyone from calling them.
It manages the urllib3 connection pool shared by all adapters, and send() is left unimplemented because pooling happens in __init__.
questions.explanation: BaseAdapter documents send() as 'Sends PreparedRequest object. Returns Response object.' and leaves send() and close() unimplemented (src/requests/adapters.py:128-155), so it acts as an interface. HTTPAdapter subclasses it and implements them (src/requests/adapters.py:158, 634). Pool management lives in HTTPAdapter.init_poolmanager, not in BaseAdapter (src/requests/adapters.py:239-267).

questions.concept: Converting a urllib3 response into a Requests Response
questions.question: After urllib3 returns a raw response, HTTPAdapter.build_response turns it into a Requests Response. Which statement best describes what happens to the data along the way?
questions.answer: Headers are wrapped in a CaseInsensitiveDict, the encoding is taken from those headers, cookies the server set are pulled into the response's cookie jar, and the raw urllib3 object is kept as response.raw.
distractors: The body is read eagerly and decoded into response.text, and the raw urllib3 object is thrown away to free the connection.
Headers are copied into a plain dict with lower-cased keys, and cookies are left on the raw response for the Session to parse later.
The adapter only copies the status code. Headers, cookies and encoding are filled in later by the Session when the user reads them.
choices: Headers are copied into a plain dict with lower-cased keys, and cookies are left on the raw response for the Session to parse later.
The body is read eagerly and decoded into response.text, and the raw urllib3 object is thrown away to free the connection.
The adapter only copies the status code. Headers, cookies and encoding are filled in later by the Session when the user reads them.

Headers are wrapped in a CaseInsensitiveDict, the encoding is taken from those headers, cookies the server set are pulled into the response's cookie jar, and the raw urllib3 object is kept as response.raw.
questions.explanation: build_response creates a Response (from models.py), wraps the headers in CaseInsensitiveDict (from structures.py), sets the encoding from those headers, keeps resp as response.raw and calls extract_cookies_to_jar (from cookies.py) (src/requests/adapters.py:376-395). The body isn't read here: response.raw keeps the urllib3 object, so the 'reads the body eagerly' and 'plain dict' options contradict the code.

questions.question: A developer creates an HTTPAdapter without passing max_retries and mounts it on a session. The first TCP connection attempt to the server fails. What happens?
questions.answer: The failure is not retried; the adapter is configured with a Retry that allows zero retries, so the error surfaces right away.
distractors: The adapter retries a few times with backoff before giving up, because connection failures are always safe to retry.
The adapter retries indefinitely until the timeout expires, since no explicit retry limit was given.
The adapter retries only if the request was a GET, because GET is idempotent.
choices: The adapter retries a few times with backoff before giving up, because connection failures are always safe to retry.
The adapter retries only if the request was a GET, because GET is idempotent.
The failure is not retried; the adapter is configured with a Retry that allows zero retries, so the error surfaces right away.
The adapter retries indefinitely until the timeout expires, since no explicit retry limit was given.
questions.explanation: When max_retries equals the default, __init__ sets self.max_retries = Retry(0, read=False) (src/requests/adapters.py:208-209), and the docstring states that by default Requests does not retry failed connections (src/requests/adapters.py:168-174). Options describing automatic or method-based retries assume behavior that only appears if you pass a custom value or Retry object.

questions.concept: Turning a urllib3 response into a Response
questions.question: A server sends the header as `content-type` (lowercase), but application code reads `response.headers['Content-Type']` and it works. Where in the flow from the low-level urllib3 response to the requests Response does this become possible?
questions.answer: In build_response, the adapter wraps the raw urllib3 headers in a CaseInsensitiveDict before assigning them to the new Response.
distractors: Response normalizes header names to title case when its headers property is first accessed.
The server's headers are lowercased by Session before the adapter sees them.
build_response copies the headers into a plain dict, and the Response class lowercases lookup keys itself.
choices: The server's headers are lowercased by Session before the adapter sees them.
build_response copies the headers into a plain dict, and the Response class lowercases lookup keys itself.
Response normalizes header names to title case when its headers property is first accessed.
In build_response, the adapter wraps the raw urllib3 headers in a CaseInsensitiveDict before assigning them to the new Response.
questions.explanation: build_response creates a fresh Response and sets response.headers = CaseInsensitiveDict(getattr(resp, 'headers', {})) under the comment 'Make headers case-insensitive' (src/requests/adapters.py:376-382). The case-insensitive behavior belongs to that data structure and is applied at the adapter boundary, not by Session or by lazy normalization in Response. The same method also attaches the raw response, the URL, cookies and the originating request (src/requests/adapters.py:386-399).

questions.concept: Case-insensitive keys that remember the last casing
questions.question: A developer runs `cid = CaseInsensitiveDict()`, then `cid['Accept'] = 'text/html'`, then `cid['ACCEPT'] = 'application/json'`. What does the dictionary hold afterwards?
questions.answer: A single entry: `list(cid)` gives `['ACCEPT']` and any casing of the key returns 'application/json'
distractors: Two separate entries, 'Accept' and 'ACCEPT', because each spelling is stored as its own key
A single entry still listed as 'Accept', because the first casing used for a key is kept forever
A single entry listed as 'accept', because every key is converted to lowercase before it is stored
choices: Two separate entries, 'Accept' and 'ACCEPT', because each spelling is stored as its own key
A single entry still listed as 'Accept', because the first casing used for a key is kept forever
A single entry: `list(cid)` gives `['ACCEPT']` and any casing of the key returns 'application/json'
A single entry listed as 'accept', because every key is converted to lowercase before it is stored
questions.explanation: `__setitem__` stores under `key.lower()` the tuple `(key, value)`, so the second assignment overwrites the same slot and replaces the remembered casing with 'ACCEPT' (src/requests/structures.py:62). `__iter__` yields that stored original key (src/requests/structures.py:71), so keys are neither duplicated nor shown in lowercase; the docstring states it remembers the case of the last key set (src/requests/structures.py:27-28).

questions.question: Code compares `CaseInsensitiveDict({'Content-Type': 'json'}) == {'content-type': 'json'}`. How does `__eq__` reach its result?
questions.answer: It wraps the plain dict in a new CaseInsensitiveDict and compares both sides' `lower_items()`, so the result is True
distractors: It compares the stored original keys directly, so the differing casing makes the result False
It returns NotImplemented because the other side is a plain dict rather than a CaseInsensitiveDict
It lowercases only its own keys and compares them with the plain dict's keys as written, so the result depends on how the other dict was typed
choices: It wraps the plain dict in a new CaseInsensitiveDict and compares both sides' `lower_items()`, so the result is True
It lowercases only its own keys and compares them with the plain dict's keys as written, so the result depends on how the other dict was typed
It returns NotImplemented because the other side is a plain dict rather than a CaseInsensitiveDict
It compares the stored original keys directly, so the differing casing makes the result False
questions.explanation: When `other` is any Mapping, `__eq__` builds `CaseInsensitiveDict(other)` and compares `dict(self.lower_items())` with `dict(other_dict.lower_items())`, so both sides are normalized to lowercase keys (src/requests/structures.py:80-86, with `lower_items` at :76-78). NotImplemented is returned only for non-Mapping values (src/requests/structures.py:83-84), so a plain dict is accepted and casing on either side does not matter.

questions.question: A Session has a default header set, and one call passes that same header key with the value None. What does merge_setting produce for that key?
questions.answer: The key is removed from the merged result, so neither the session value nor None is sent
distractors: The session's value is kept because None means 'no override'
The header is sent with an empty string as its value
merge_setting raises an error because a mapping value cannot be None
choices: The key is removed from the merged result, so neither the session value nor None is sent
The session's value is kept because None means 'no override'
The header is sent with an empty string as its value
merge_setting raises an error because a mapping value cannot be None
questions.explanation: merge_setting starts from the session mapping, applies the request mapping on top, then deletes every key whose merged value is None (src/requests/sessions.py:96-103). So passing None is how a caller turns off a session default for a single request. The session value is not kept, because the request's None overwrites it before the cleanup step.

questions.question: A developer sets s.headers['User-Agent'] = 'app/1' on a Session and then calls s.get(url, headers={'user-agent': 'probe'}). Which User-Agent is sent, and where is that decided?
questions.answer: 'probe' is sent: Session.request builds a Request, and prepare_request merges headers with merge_setting into a CaseInsensitiveDict, where the per-request value overrides the session value
distractors: 'app/1' is sent, because session headers are applied after the request is prepared
Both values are sent, because the keys differ in case and are stored as separate headers
'probe' is sent, but only because the adapter replaces session headers right before transmission
choices: Both values are sent, because the keys differ in case and are stored as separate headers
'probe' is sent: Session.request builds a Request, and prepare_request merges headers with merge_setting into a CaseInsensitiveDict, where the per-request value overrides the session value
'probe' is sent, but only because the adapter replaces session headers right before transmission
'app/1' is sent, because session headers are applied after the request is prepared
questions.explanation: Session.request wraps the arguments in a Request and calls prepare_request (src/requests/sessions.py:623-635). There, the headers are merged with merge_setting(request.headers, self.headers, dict_class=CaseInsensitiveDict) (src/requests/sessions.py:547-549). merge_setting builds the result from the session mapping first and then updates it with the request mapping (src/requests/sessions.py:96-97). Because the merged dict ignores case, 'user-agent' and 'User-Agent' are the same key, so the headers are not sent twice.

questions.question: A teammate writes `with requests.Session() as s:` instead of creating a Session and leaving it around. What does the `with` form add?
questions.answer: When the block exits, the session's close() is called automatically, so its resources are released even if an error occurs inside the block
distractors: Each request inside the block gets a fresh, empty cookie jar so state never leaks between calls
The session's settings are locked, so headers and auth cannot be changed inside the block
Requests inside the block are sent in parallel and joined when the block exits
choices: The session's settings are locked, so headers and auth cannot be changed inside the block
Each request inside the block gets a fresh, empty cookie jar so state never leaks between calls
When the block exits, the session's close() is called automatically, so its resources are released even if an error occurs inside the block
Requests inside the block are sent in parallel and joined when the block exits
questions.explanation: __enter__ simply returns the session and __exit__ calls self.close() (src/requests/sessions.py:505-509), so cleanup happens on any exit from the block. Nothing in these methods resets cookies, freezes settings, or changes how requests are sent; the cookie jar is shared across the session (src/requests/sessions.py:498).

questions.question: A developer builds a `Request(...)` object and passes it straight to `session.send()`. What happens, and what is the intended path?
questions.answer: send raises ValueError; the Request must first become a PreparedRequest (via prepare_request, which merges in session settings), as Session.request does before calling send
distractors: send silently prepares it but skips the session's headers and cookies
send accepts it and the HTTPAdapter turns it into a PreparedRequest just before sending
send raises InvalidSchema because a plain Request has no URL scheme yet
choices: send raises ValueError; the Request must first become a PreparedRequest (via prepare_request, which merges in session settings), as Session.request does before calling send
send accepts it and the HTTPAdapter turns it into a PreparedRequest just before sending
send raises InvalidSchema because a plain Request has no URL scheme yet
send silently prepares it but skips the session's headers and cookies
questions.explanation: send explicitly guards `if isinstance(request, Request): raise ValueError("You can only send PreparedRequests.")` (src/requests/sessions.py:765-768). Session.request builds a Request, calls prepare_request to produce a PreparedRequest with merged session headers, cookies, auth and hooks, then calls send (src/requests/sessions.py:623-651, 540-555). InvalidSchema comes from get_adapter, not from this check.

questions.question: A developer calls register_hook with an event name the object was not set up to handle (for example a typo like "respnse"). What does the hooks mixin do?
questions.answer: It raises a ValueError naming the unsupported event, so the typo is caught immediately
distractors: It creates a new empty hook list for that event name and appends the hook
It silently ignores the hook and returns without changing anything
It registers the hook under the default "response" event instead
choices: It raises a ValueError naming the unsupported event, so the typo is caught immediately
It registers the hook under the default "response" event instead
It silently ignores the hook and returns without changing anything
It creates a new empty hook list for that event name and appends the hook
questions.explanation: register_hook first checks that the event already exists in self.hooks and raises ValueError with the event name if not (src/requests/models.py:262-263). It never creates new event keys, so a misspelled event fails loudly instead of registering a hook that would never fire.

questions.question: What happens when you call prepare() on a user-created Request object?
questions.answer: A new PreparedRequest is created and filled from the Request's fields; the Request itself keeps its raw inputs and can be prepared again
distractors: The Request converts itself in place into the wire-ready form, so its original fields are replaced
The Request sends itself to the server and returns a Response
The Request copies its fields into a shared PreparedRequest cached on the class
choices: The Request sends itself to the server and returns a Response
The Request converts itself in place into the wire-ready form, so its original fields are replaced
A new PreparedRequest is created and filled from the Request's fields; the Request itself keeps its raw inputs and can be prepared again
The Request copies its fields into a shared PreparedRequest cached on the class
questions.explanation: Request.prepare builds a fresh PreparedRequest() and passes method, url, headers, files, data, json, params, auth, cookies and hooks into its prepare method, then returns it (src/requests/models.py:360-375). The Request is only a holder of user inputs; normalization (upper-cased method, encoded URL, CaseInsensitiveDict headers) happens on the PreparedRequest (src/requests/models.py:424-451). Sending is not part of prepare().

concepts.name: requests.get() to HTTP request, sessions and adapters
concepts.definition: How a top-level call such as requests.get() is routed through the api module into a Session, how Session merges per-request and session-level settings, and where adapters fit in the sending path.

items.caption: Read api.py: get() is a thin wrapper, and request() owns a short-lived Session.

questions.question: What does requests.get(url, params=...) actually do with the call?
questions.answer: It forwards to request() with the method string "get" and the same params and kwargs.
distractors: It opens a socket itself and writes the GET line directly.
It builds a Response object by itself without any other function.
It looks up a cached Session shared by all module-level calls.
questions.explanation: get() ends with `return request("get", url, params=params, **kwargs)`, so it only delegates. The other options attribute work to get() that it does not do.

questions.question: Why does request() use a `with sessions.Session() as session:` block?
questions.answer: So the session is closed when the call finishes, avoiding leftover open sockets and ResourceWarnings.
distractors: So the session's cookies are saved for the next top-level call.
So the request is sent asynchronously in the background.
So redirects are disabled for the call.
questions.explanation: The comment at api.py:67-69 says the with statement ensures the session is closed to avoid open sockets. Nothing there persists state or changes redirects.

items.caption: Read merge_setting in sessions.py: how a request's settings combine with the session's.

questions.question: A session has a timeout-like setting configured, but a particular request passes None for it. What does merge_setting return?
questions.answer: The session's setting.
distractors: None, because the request value wins.
An empty OrderedDict.
It raises an error because the values conflict.
questions.explanation: `if request_setting is None: return session_setting` (sessions.py:87-88). The request value only takes priority when it is not None.

questions.question: Session headers and request headers are both mappings. How does merge_setting combine them?
questions.answer: It copies the session's items, then updates them with the request's items so request values override on the same key.
distractors: It returns only the request headers and drops the session ones.
It returns only the session headers and ignores the request ones.
It concatenates values of the same key into one string.
questions.explanation: Lines 96-97 build a dict from session_setting and call update with request_setting, so request wins on collisions while other session keys remain.

items.caption: Follow requests.get() into Session: what the module-level call creates and returns.

questions.question: Trace requests.get(url): which sequence matches the code?
questions.answer: get() calls request("get", ...), which creates a Session and calls session.request(method=..., url=..., **kwargs), returning its Response.
distractors: get() calls Session.get on a module-level Session created at import time.
get() builds a PreparedRequest itself and hands it to an adapter.
get() calls session.send directly and request() is only used for POST.
questions.explanation: api.py:87 delegates to request, and api.py:70-71 creates a Session and returns session.request(...). Preparing and sending happen inside the session, not in api.py.

questions.question: A developer calls requests.get(a) then requests.get(b) expecting cookies set by the first response to be sent with the second. What explains why that is not guaranteed by this code?
questions.answer: Each top-level call creates and closes its own Session, and sessions are what persist cookies, auth and proxies.
distractors: get() strips cookies from every response before returning it.
Cookies are only supported for POST requests.
The api module keeps a single global Session but resets it after each call.
questions.explanation: The sessions module docstring says Session persists settings such as cookies across requests, while api.py:70 makes a new Session per call inside a with block.

items.caption: Why merge_hooks exists next to merge_setting, and how non-mapping settings are handled.

questions.question: Why does merge_hooks return one side early when the other has an empty 'response' list, instead of always calling merge_setting?
questions.answer: Because merging {'response': []} through merge_setting would break the session's hooks, so the non-empty side is returned directly.
distractors: Because hooks must never be merged, only the session's hooks are ever used.
Because empty lists are invalid and raise an error in merge_setting.
Because merge_hooks must always prefer the request hooks over session hooks.
questions.explanation: The docstring at sessions.py:113-116 states that when request_hooks == {'response': []} the merge breaks Session hooks entirely, hence the early returns.

questions.question: A session sets verify to one value and a request sets a different non-mapping value. What does merge_setting return, and why?
questions.answer: The request's value, because the merge is bypassed when either side is not a Mapping.
distractors: The session's value, because session settings are authoritative.
A dict containing both values.
None, because the two values conflict.
questions.explanation: Lines 90-94 return request_setting if the two are not both Mappings (the comment mentions verify). Only dict-like settings are merged key by key.

items.caption: Design trade-off: a fresh Session per top-level call versus a shared one.

questions.question: Suppose api.request were changed to reuse one module-level Session for all requests.get() calls. Which consequence follows from the Session's role shown in the code?
questions.answer: Cookies, auth and other settings persisted on that Session would leak between unrelated calls, and the closing guarantee of the with block would be lost.
distractors: Nothing would change, since Session stores no state between requests.
Per-request keyword arguments would stop being merged with session settings.
get() would no longer be able to return a Response object.
questions.explanation: sessions.py documents that Session persists cookies, auth and proxies, and api.py:67-71 uses a with block per call to close it. A shared session would carry state across callers and never be closed per call.

questions.concept: Shared code path for verb helpers
questions.question: get() and options() both end by calling request(). What design benefit does this give when a new keyword such as a new transport option must be supported?
questions.answer: It needs to be handled only in the request path through Session, and every verb helper that forwards **kwargs picks it up.
distractors: Each verb helper must be edited separately to forward it.
Only get() can accept it because it has an explicit params argument.
It must be added to the Response class so helpers can return it.
questions.explanation: api.py:87 and api.py:99 both forward **kwargs to request(), which forwards them to session.request, so helpers share one path rather than duplicating logic.

items.caption: What would break if merge_hooks lacked its guards, and how None unsets session defaults.

questions.question: If the early-return guards in merge_hooks were removed and it always called merge_setting, what would happen when the session has {'response': [hook]} and the request passes {'response': []}?
questions.answer: The request's empty list would overwrite the session's 'response' key, so the session's hook would silently not run.
distractors: The two lists would be concatenated so the hook runs once.
merge_setting would raise a TypeError for list values.
The session's hook would run twice.
questions.explanation: merge_setting copies session items then updates with request items (sessions.py:96-97), so the same key from the request replaces the session's value, which is the breakage described at lines 115-116.

questions.question: What capability does the loop that deletes keys whose value is None in merge_setting give callers?
questions.answer: A request can pass None for a key to suppress a default that the session would otherwise send.
distractors: It lets the session delete its own defaults permanently.
It prevents the request from overriding any session key.
It converts None values into empty strings.
questions.explanation: After merging, keys with None values are removed (sessions.py:99-103), so a per-request None overrides the session value and then drops the key from the merged result.
